milestones.title: Baekje founds Wiryeseong
milestones.detail: According to the Samguk Sagi, Onjo founds the kingdom later called Baekje at Wiryeseong in 18 BC. The earthen walls of Pungnap Toseong and Mongchon Toseong in south-eastern Seoul are believed to be its remains.

milestones.title: Goguryeo captures the Baekje capital
milestones.detail: King Jangsu of Goguryeo takes Wiryeseong and the Han River basin and kills King Gaero. Baekje moves its capital south to Ungjin (Gongju).

milestones.title: Silla takes the Han River basin
milestones.detail: Silla seizes the region from Baekje and makes it a frontier province. The name Hanyang comes into use during the Unified Silla period.

milestones.title: Goryeo builds its Southern Capital, Namgyeong
milestones.detail: King Sukjong of Goryeo builds a palace near the site of the later Gyeongbokgung and names the town Namgyeong, the Southern Capital. Seoul grows into a sizeable town from this period.

milestones.title: Joseon moves its capital to Hanyang
milestones.detail: King Taejo chooses Hanyang as the capital of the new Joseon dynasty and the court moves there in the tenth lunar month of 1394. Gyeongbokgung Palace and the Jongmyo shrine are built in 1394-95.
milestones.source: Veritable Records of King Taejo, https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kaa_10310025_001 , via https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/서울특별시의_역사 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Seoul

milestones.title: City wall and eight gates built
milestones.detail: Work on the Seoul City Wall begins in 1395 and most of it, with the eight gates, is finished in 1396. The wall runs about 18.6 km along the ridges of the four inner mountains.

milestones.title: Japanese invasion; the palaces burn
milestones.detail: Japanese forces take the city in 1592. All of Seoul's palaces are burned, and Gyeongbokgung lies in ruins until it is rebuilt in 1865-68.

milestones.title: Gyeongbokgung rebuilt
milestones.detail: The regent Heungseon Daewongun completes the reconstruction of Gyeongbokgung Palace, begun in 1865, restoring the main palace after more than 270 years.

milestones.title: Railway reaches Seoul
milestones.detail: The Incheon-Seoul railway begins operating in 1900. Electric trams and electric lighting arrive in the same years under the Korean Empire.

milestones.title: Annexation: Hanseong becomes Keijō
milestones.detail: Japan annexes Korea and makes Seoul the colonial capital. On 1 October 1910 Hanseong-bu is renamed Gyeongseong-bu (Keijō) and placed under Gyeonggi Province; in 1914 its area is cut back to the walled city and Yongsan.

milestones.title: City limits extended fourfold
milestones.detail: Keijō annexes Yeongdeungpo south of the Han River and districts to the east and west, growing to about 134-136 square kilometres, four times its 1914 area.

milestones.title: Seoul Special City
milestones.detail: After liberation in 1945 the city takes the name Seoul and in 1948 becomes capital of the Republic of Korea. In 1949 it is made a special city and its area is doubled.

milestones.title: Korean War
milestones.detail: Seoul falls on 28 June 1950, is retaken in September, lost again in January 1951 and recovered in March 1951. A wartime count in March 1953 finds about 750,000 residents, half the 1949 figure.

milestones.title: Great expansion south of the Han
milestones.detail: On 1 January 1963 parts of Gyeonggi Province are merged into Seoul, expanding its area 2.3 times to 613 square kilometres, close to today's limits. Development of Yeouido and Gangnam follows.
milestones.source: Seoul Metropolitan Government, Seoul Solution, 'Changes to Seoul's Administrative Districts and Development of Urban Space', https://seoulsolution.kr/ ; https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/서울특별시의_역사

milestones.title: Subway opens
milestones.detail: Seoul Subway Line 1 begins operating on 15 August 1974.

milestones.title: Summer Olympics; ten million people
milestones.detail: Seoul hosts the 1988 Summer Olympics. The city's population passes ten million the same year.

notes: Start date is contested and should be reviewed. 18 BC is the traditional date in the 12th-century Samguk Sagi for the founding of the Baekje capital Wiryeseong; the city government's own history counts Seoul's 2,000 years from it, and it is marked estimated, not documented. That capital stood at Pungnap Toseong and Mongchon Toseong in today's Songpa district (about 37.530 N, 127.116 E), roughly 13 km south-east of the later centre, and fell in 475. The present city centre has a separate, securely documented beginning: a Goryeo palace town called Namgyeong from 1104, and the Joseon capital Hanyang from 1394. If the project prefers the founding of the continuous city on its present site, use 1394 (or 1104). The historic_core given is the Joseon walled city, because that is what the modern city grew out from; it is not the Baekje site. Population: nothing was found for the 1,400 years before 1428, so the series starts there. Joseon figures are household-register totals for Hanseong-bu (walled city plus outer districts), which mostly counted taxable adults; Seoul's historians put the real population at 250,000-300,000 from the mid-17th century and about 340,000 in the 1860s, so the points for 1648-1835 are low. The 1750 and 1800 points are Chandler's and follow the same registers. Colonial figures cover Keijō as bounded at each date (reduced in 1914, enlarged in 1936); the 1915, 1935 and 1944 values are rounded and the two sources for 1936 disagree (636,000 and about 730,000). The individual colonial census counts for 1925, 1930 and 1940 could not be sourced and are left out. The UN series from 1950 covers the wider urban agglomeration. Landmarks: no sourced height was found for the main Joseon monuments, so Sungnyemun (Namdaemun, 1398), Heunginjimun (Dongdaemun), Gyeongbokgung's Geunjeongjeon throne hall and Gwanghwamun, the Seoul City Wall, the Government-General Building (1926, demolished 1995-96), Seoul Station (1925) and the Olympic Stadium (1984) are left out. Namsan Seoul Tower's 236 m is the height of the structure itself, not counting the hill it stands on.
